narrative:
After carefully reviewing your application, the admissions system flagged a meaningful concern about your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, estimating your probability of not passing at 51%. While this is a close call, it was ultimately enough to result in a rejection, and we want to make sure you understand exactly what drove that outcome so you can take meaningful steps forward.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your academic performance during your third year of law school, where your grades placed you in the 1st decile within your school — meaning nearly all of your peers performed above you at that stage. Students who go on to pass the bar exam are, on average, in roughly the 6th decile by their third year, so this gap is significant. Third-year performance is particularly telling because it reflects how well a student has consolidated their legal knowledge heading into the final stretch before the bar, and in your case, this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward a concern about passing. Your first-year academic standing told a similar story, with grades also placing you in the lower range compared to successful students, reinforcing the pattern seen in your third year.

That said, the picture is not entirely discouraging. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is notably strong — well above the 3.24 average among students who passed the bar — and this actually worked in your favor, pulling the prediction back toward a more optimistic outcome. Similarly, your LSAT score of 34, while somewhat below the average of 37 among students who passed, also contributed modestly in a positive direction. These two factors together show that you have real academic ability and potential, which is why the decision was so close.

The challenge is that your law school performance, particularly in your later years, did not yet reflect that underlying potential. Studying part-time may have made it harder to stay fully engaged with coursework, and this is worth reflecting on as you plan your next steps. We strongly encourage you to consider retaking the LSAT to bring your score closer to or above the average, and more importantly, to explore what contributed to the decline in your law school grades over time and address those factors directly. Speaking with an academic advisor, enrolling in a bar preparation course, or even considering a full-time study arrangement could meaningfully improve your standing in a future application.
